title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: Stateless Core, Apps & Tasks
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol project finalized the **2026-07-28 specification**, the most significant revision to MCP since its November 2024 launch. It followed a ten-week release-candidate window and lands four major changes: a stateless core transport, a versioned extensions framework (starting with MCP Apps and Tasks), hardened OAuth/OIDC authorization, and a formal deprecation policy for older mechanisms. Claude and Claude Code have expanded support for the new spec.

---

## Stateless Core

Previous MCP versions required an `initialize`/`initialized` handshake and tracked session state via an `Mcp-Session-Id` header, meaning a client and server had to maintain a stateful connection across the interaction. The 2026-07-28 spec removes both:

- No more handshake — a client can issue a request against a server without first negotiating a session
- Routing moves to headers instead of an established session
- `list` and resource-read results are now explicitly **cacheable**, since there's no session state that could make a cached result stale

This matters for scale: stateless servers are far easier to run behind standard HTTP load balancers and horizontally scale, since any request can be routed to any server instance.

---

## Versioned Extensions: Apps and Tasks

Rather than keep growing the core protocol, new capabilities now ship as **versioned extensions** with their own release cadence:

### MCP Apps
Server-rendered, interactive HTML interfaces that run inside sandboxed iframes. Tools declare their UI templates up front, which lets clients **prefetch** the UI and run a security review on it before ever invoking the tool — closing a gap where a tool's rendered output couldn't be vetted ahead of time.

### Tasks
A redesigned model for long-running work, replacing ad hoc polling patterns with three defined operations:
- `tasks/get` — poll-based status check
- `tasks/update` — push a progress update
- `tasks/cancel` — cooperative cancellation (the task can decline or need time to wind down, rather than being killed outright)

---

## OAuth/OIDC Authorization Hardening

Six Specification Enhancement Proposals (SEPs) landed in this release, each closing a specific gap in MCP's existing OAuth 2.1 authorization flow as it met real deployed practice — for example around token audience restriction and client registration edge cases. The goal is to bring MCP's auth story in line with how OAuth/OIDC is actually run in production identity systems, rather than a simplified subset.

---

## Deprecation Policy

The spec formalizes a deprecation lifecycle for the first time:

- **Roots, Sampling, Logging, and Dynamic Client Registration (DCR):** minimum 12-month deprecation window before removal
- **HTTP+SSE transport:** follows its own separately published removal schedule, distinct from the 12-month default

This gives server and client authors a predictable timeline instead of features disappearing without notice.

---

## Why It Matters

Before this release, every MCP deployment had to carry the complexity of session lifecycle management even for simple, stateless tool calls — one of the friction points that made MCP servers harder to deploy at scale than a plain REST API. Combined with the versioned extensions model, the 2026-07-28 spec lets the core protocol stay small and stable while Apps, Tasks, and future capabilities evolve independently. See the [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents) page for how MCP fits into Claude's broader agentic tool-use model.
